segments.title: The scenario and the profile
sections: The Profile, Value And The POC

cues.text: Twelve lines on the chart, and no plan. The prior session's high and low, a value area, a point of control, a few nodes from last week.
Price comes into one of them and you do not know whether to expect a stop, a turn or a slice straight through.
So you wait for the bar to tell you, and by the time it does, the trade has gone. The problem is not too many lines. It is lines with no job.
This module reads the volume profile as an auction. Every item ends in a line on your plan that names a target or a regime. Never a direction.
The auction belongs to the setup. It supplies locations and targets, and it informs the read. It is never the trigger.
Now, the profile. A price chart shows price over time. A volume profile turns the chart on its side and shows how much traded at each price.
Wide rows are prices where the market did a lot of business. Thin rows are prices it passed through quickly.
Three names to know. The point of control, or POC, is the single price with the most volume. Built from volume it is the VPOC, and the prior session's VPOC is the level PD VPOC.
The value area is the band around it that holds a set share of the session's volume, by convention about 70 percent.
Its edges are VAH and VAL, the value area high and low. The prior session's edges are the levels PD VAH and PD VAL. Marked, they are locations and targets, never triggers.
The rule: mark PD VAH, PD VAL and PD VPOC from the 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern profile, built one way, and write the session and the build on the level line.
Platforms build value two ways: from volume at each price, or from time at each price, called TPO. A time build gives a TPO POC, not a VPOC. Mixing them is the mistake.
Getting it wrong is a value area from a full-session profile one day and a regular-hours one the next. The levels came from whatever the screen showed. The screen is not a methodology.
The fix: save one profile template and draw prior-session levels only from it. Every level line carries its source: PD VAH, 21,432, regular hours, volume.

check.q: What does a volume profile show that a price chart does not?
options: How much traded at each price
check.why: It turns the chart on its side to show volume at each price: wide rows were accepted, thin rows were passed through.

check.q: Which price is the POC?
options: The first price of the session
The midpoint of the session's range
The price with the most volume traded
check.why: The point of control is the single price where the most volume traded.

check.q: Your PD VAH came from a regular-hours volume profile and your POC from a time-based chart. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, both are the prior session
The two levels were built two ways
check.why: Volume and time builds can give different edges on the same day. Mixing them is the mistake; pick one and write it on the line.

check.q: Levels drawn off whatever the screen showed reveal what?
options: The levels came from the screen, not from a definition
The levels are too close together
check.why: Without one template you cannot tell a level that failed from a level drawn somewhere else.

cues.text: An auction does one of two things. Either both sides keep trading around a price they agree on, or one side is in charge and price moves to find the other.
The first is balance. Price rotates around an agreed price, inside edges both sides defend. Value areas from one session to the next overlap.
The second is imbalance. One side is in charge, and value migrates: each session's value area sits beyond the last, with little or no overlap.
In balance, the middle is where both sides agree, so there is nothing to be had there. The edges are where something can happen.

In imbalance, the old edges are behind price, and what matters is whether value follows it. Price that leaves and builds no volume has not been accepted. Price that builds value beyond the old edge has.

Value migration is the plainest read the profile gives you. Value areas stepping higher, session after session, is acceptance at higher prices. Overlapping value areas are balance, whatever the candles looked like.
Choppy is usually balance nobody named. The chart was not confusing. It was unlabelled.
The rule: name the regime before you name a trade, in one line, with the price that would end it.
For example: balance, 21,340 to 21,432, ends on acceptance outside either edge. Or: imbalance up, value higher three sessions, ends on acceptance back inside the prior session's value.
Getting it wrong is trading the middle of a balance, or fading every new high in an auction whose value has moved up three sessions running.
It reveals that the trade was read off the last few bars, and the regime they sat in was never named.
The fix: the regime line is the first line under your levels. Before any entry, read it back. If you cannot say which regime the trade sits in, the trade is not taken.

segments.title: Nodes: where price slows, where it runs
sections: HVN And LVN: Where Price Slows, Where It Runs

cues.text: Zoom out from one session to a profile of several, and the same shapes repeat at a larger scale. Wide sections where many sessions did business, and thin gaps between them.
A wide section is a high volume node, an HVN. Think of a crowd. Price that reaches it tends to slow down and rotate.
A thin section is a low volume node, an LVN. Think of an empty corridor. Price crossed it quickly the first time, and with no business to hold it, it tends to cross quickly again.
That gives you the path between any entry and any target.
One: an HVN in the way means price has to work through agreement to get there.
Two: an LVN in the way means nothing stops it except the next node.
Three: if price is accepted beyond the edge of an HVN, the next HVN across the LVN becomes the next target.
The rule: for every target you write, list the nodes between the entry and the target.
Next to the target, write the path in one short phrase. Via LVN 21,300 to 21,322. Or: through HVN 21,380 to 21,396.
A target with no path written beside it is not a target yet.
Getting it wrong is a target three nodes away with two HVNs in between that the plan never mentioned. Or a trade held in the middle of an LVN, waiting for price to settle there.
An LVN is where price does not stay. That is the whole definition.
It reveals that the profile was read for its lines, not its shape, so the path was never part of the plan. Which nodes count as levels in their own right is Module 6.

segments.title: The open and unfinished business
sections: The Open Relative To Prior Value

cues.text: At 9:30 a.m. the regular session opens somewhere against the prior session's auction. Where it opens decides which levels are near. It does not decide which way price goes.
One: in value, between PD VAL and PD VAH. The targets are PD VPOC, then the value edge on each side.
Two: above value, inside the prior range but over PD VAH. The targets are PD VAH below, and PD High, the prior session's high, above.
Three: below value, inside the range but under PD VAL. The targets are PD VAL above, and PD Low below.
Four: a gap, outside the prior range altogether. The target is the range edge. Module 12 covers it.
The rule: at 9:30 a.m., write one word for where the open sits, and the targets it puts in play. Never a direction. Never a reason to enter.

Getting it wrong is "opened in value, so it is going to the POC," followed by an entry from the middle of nowhere. A target was used as a trigger. Price visits plenty of places. That does not make them good trades.
The fix: the open line has two fields, the location word and the targets. There is no direction field.
Now, unfinished business. Every auction ends at an extreme, and how it ends tells you whether it finished.
Excess is a tail of thin, quickly traded prints. Price reached the extreme, found the other side waiting, and left fast. That end finished.
A poor high has no tail. Price stopped flat, often at the same price in two or more 30-minute periods. It stopped without being refused.

The rule: carried onto the next session's plan, a poor high or poor low is unfinished business, marked UB. It goes on the target line only, where a trade you already have can aim. Never the reason to open one.
Getting it wrong is buying the open because that poor high has to be repaired. The target became the thesis.
The fix: if the only line supporting an entry is a UB line, the entry has no location, and it is not taken.

segments.title: Open types and the worked case
sections: Open Types, And The Wish To Know The Day
Worked Case: Reading One Profile Three Ways

cues.text: Traders have names for what the first minutes of the session do. They are useful words. Each describes something that has already happened.
An open drive leaves the opening price at once and does not trade back. An open test drive probes one way, turns, and drives the other way.
An open rejection reverse moves away, meets the other side, and rotates back through the open. An open auction rotates around the open.
The pull is not technical. At 9:35 a.m. you want to know what kind of day it is, because knowing would make every decision easy.
An open drive feels like a trend day. An open auction feels like a range. The label is satisfying. It is a caption, not a forecast.

The rule: open types and day types are words for what happened. Neither goes on your plan as a call for the day. Your plan carries an idea instead: thesis, invalidation and conviction, at a named level.
Getting it wrong is "open drive, so trend day, so hold everything." The need for certainty was met with a label, and the label then did the trading.
The fix: your plan has no day-type field. Strike any day-type word out and write the level that would prove the idea wrong. If you cannot name one, the line was a wish.
Now, the worked case. A composite profile, invented prices. It stops before any trade: no entry, no stop, no outcome.
The prior high, 21,480, is flat, touched in two 30-minute periods: a poor high. Value runs from 21,340 to 21,432, with the point of control at 21,388, inside an HVN.
Below value, an LVN from 21,300 to 21,322, crossed twice, quickly. The low, 21,262, finished with excess.
The regime line: this value overlaps the session before. Balance, 21,340 to 21,432, ends on acceptance outside either edge. The poor high goes on the target line as UB at 21,480.
Three opens against that profile. Open one, 21,404, in value: PD VPOC at 21,388 is 16 points away, inside the HVN, so price is expected to slow there.
Open two, 21,450, above value: PD VAH is 18 points below, PD High and UB 30 points above.
Open three, 21,495, a gap above the prior high: the target is the range edge, 21,480, 15 points. The UB sits on the same price.
None of the three opens says which way price goes, and none of the targets is an entry.

sections: Can You Read The Auction Before 09:30?

cues.text: Can you read the auction before 9:30 a.m.? Take the prior session's chart and the plan you wrote for your next session, or write one now. Score one point for each line that is on the plan, in writing.
One: value. PD VAH, PD VAL and PD VPOC, with the session and the build beside them.
Two: regime. Balance or imbalance, with the price that would end it.
Three: path. For each target, the HVNs and LVNs between the open and the target.
Four: the open. One word for where it sat, and the targets it put in play.
Five: unfinished business. Any poor high or low from the prior session, on the target line and nowhere else.
Six: no call. No direction taken from the open, and no day-type word, anywhere on the plan.

Six of six: the auction is on your plan as it should be. Four or five: write the missing lines before your next session. Under four: no trade at a profile level until all six are written for that day.
One line overrides the score. If line six fails, treat the plan as under four, whatever the total. A plan with a day call on it is a horoscope with price levels.

Before your next session, write one line: the prior session's VAH, VAL and VPOC from the 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern profile. At 9:30 a.m., add one word, in value, above value, below value or gap, and the two nearest targets.
No direction. That is the whole assignment.

Where it goes next. Module 6 takes the profile levels from here and decides which go on your level list, and how each one's session scope is written. Module 12 picks up the fourth open, outside the prior range.

The regime line and the target line feed the setup read in Modules 10 and 11. The open line is part of the morning sheet in Module 16. And the idea that replaces a day call is taught in Module 9, and made a daily habit in Module 19.

check.q: Your plan scores 6 of 6 but line six fails. How do you treat it?
check.why: A call for the day will override every other line, so a failed line six means the plan is treated as under 4.

check.q: What does the open line on your plan hold?
options: A day type and a target
A location word and a direction
A location word and the targets
check.why: Two fields only. There is no direction field.

check.q: A score of 4 or 5 means what?
options: Write the missing lines before your next session
No trade at a profile level
check.why: Under 4 means no trade at a profile level; 4 or 5 means write the missing lines first.

check.q: Which module decides which profile levels go on your level list?
check.why: Module 6, What Counts As A Level, takes the profile levels from this one.

questions.q: What does a volume profile show?
options: How much traded at each price
questions.why: It shows volume at each price: where the market agreed and where it passed through.

questions.q: Why is a TPO POC mixed with a volume-built VAH wrong?
options: The two were built two ways, so they cannot be compared
A VAH is not a level
questions.why: Neither build is wrong. Mixing them is. Pick one and write it on the line.

questions.q: Value areas overlap from session to session. What is the regime?
questions.why: Overlapping value is balance, whatever the candles looked like.

questions.q: Price is accepted beyond the edge of an HVN, across an LVN. What is the next target?
options: The next HVN across the LVN
questions.why: The far side of an LVN is where price is expected to arrive: the next HVN.

questions.q: Which belongs on the target line, marked UB?
options: A poor high or poor low
questions.why: Unfinished business is a poor high or low carried onto the next plan, as a target only.

questions.q: What does the open line on your plan hold?
options: A direction and a day type
A location word and the targets it puts in play
questions.why: One word for where the open sits, and the targets in play. No direction field.

questions.q: Where does an open type such as "open drive" belong?
options: As vocabulary for what happened, never a call
questions.why: Open types and day types are words for what happened.

questions.q: What does every item in this module end in?
options: A target or regime line, never a direction
questions.why: The auction belongs to the setup: locations, targets and the read. It is never the trigger.
